title: Platform Ops Guardian — positioning brief
body:
Purpose and intent:
This one-pager is a compact, tactical framing for how we tell platform and infra buyers why Redwood matters when the ask is not just model access but predictable, auditable, and low-friction inference operations. Use for sales prep, SDR outreach experiments, and as the starting script for technical win narratives.

Top-line thesis (one sentence):
Redwood turns inference from a brittle engineering project into platform-grade operational plumbing—making LLM features predictable, measurable, and inexpensive to run at scale.

Why this narrative (context):
- We increasingly compete against two vectors: model-access sellers who sell capability and self-host efforts that sell control. Neither addresses the day‑to‑day ops overhead (latency spikes, cost drift, silent regressions, rollout risk) that actually breaks product SLAs.
- Platform teams buy against operational risk and the cost of unknowns. They want to minimize human intervention and have clear levers when performance or cost changes.
- Positioning Redwood as the “Guardian” of inference operations highlights reliability, observable economics, and safe evolution of models.

Core positioning pillars (short statements to build messaging from):
1) Operationalized inference: standardized routing, safe rollouts, canaries, automatic fallback.
2) Unit economics you can act on: per-token costing, batching/cache knobs surfaced as policies rather than guesswork.
3) Observable trust: token-level traces, model-level quality alerts, audit trails for compliance.
4) Flexible deployment: same controls across hosted, reserved (Dedicated), and private installs.
5) De-risked upgrades: model variants + automated compatibility fallbacks to keep apps running.

Primary buyer personas and their pain language:
- Platform/Infrastructure Lead (platform teams): "We cannot afford random latency spikes or unknown runaway costs across teams."
- ML/Model Ops Lead: "Deploying a new model is a risky experiment; I need confidence it won’t regress production signals."
- Product/Engineering Manager: "Users experience tail latency and inconsistent replies—this kills feature adoption."
- Security/Compliance Lead: "We need auditability, VPC controls, and provable data isolation for regulated data."

Key messages mapped to buyers (snappy lines):
- Platform: "Put inference on autopilot—predictable throughput and controlled costs without hand‑holding."
- ML/Ops: "Ship model iterations safely: canaries, automatic rollbacks, and quality regression alerts."
- Eng/Product: "Consistent real‑world latency and availability for your LLM features—across regions and traffic patterns."
- Security: "Run inference where your data lives with full audit logs and KMS integration."

Proof points we can (and should) use quickly:
- Runtime architecture: continuous batching + KV cache reduces per‑token latency and cost (quantified in later docs).
- Rolling upgrades: internal case where canary + auto-fallback prevented an outage during a model swap (reference: ops postmortem Q3 2024).
- Dedicated contracts: customers with reserved pools saw 3x throughput predictability vs ephemeral endpoints.
- Observability: token-level traces and regression alerts surfaced a subtle prompt drift issue that saved an enterprise customer from a month of silent quality loss.

Competitive framing (how to win vs alternatives):
- Vs. "Model-access" APIs: They sell capabilities; we sell operational guarantees. If your metric is uptime, latency SLOs, or cost-per-session, capability alone isn’t enough.
- Vs. self-hosted stacks: They promise control but impose heavy ongoing ops. We deliver control points (private deployment + VPC) without the full maintenance tax—standardized tooling and woefully fewer maintenance cycles.
- Vs. other inference platforms: We combine runtime-level optimizations with product-grade controls (rollouts, tracing, economics dashboard) in one developer experience.

Elevator pitch (30s):
"Redwood makes inference operational. Instead of treating LLMs as experiments, we give platform and product teams the controls and visibility to run them like a core service—predictable latency, measurable unit economics, and safe upgrades across hosted or private environments."

One-line SVP for execs: 
"Redwood protects your product by turning inference into a manageable, auditable service—not a monthly firefight."

Suggested GTM plays (quick experiments):
1) Platform postmortem playbook outreach: short checklist + webinar for platform teams about preventing inference outages.
2) Cost-savings calculator: ask users for traffic profile, show predicted token-cost delta with Redwood batching/caching.
3) Migration sprint offer: a 6‑week assisted migration for Dedicated or Private with SLA-backed throughput targets.
4) Compliance brief: target security-led RFPs with audit log + KMS reference architecture.

Risks and unresolved counters (notes to iterate on):
- Customers will push back: "We can run this ourselves." Need tight TCO and ops-time data to quantify the ongoing burden.
- "Vendor lock-in" angle for private deployments—be explicit about exportable config and migration patterns.
- Latency skeptics will want end-to-end benchmarks across regions and p99 metrics for long contexts.

Open questions for product/eng (items to chase before go‑wide):
- Can we produce a standard TCO comparison template that maps to platform team KPIs (MTTR, ops hours, cost volatility)?
- Are there 2–3 customer stories with quantified impact (cost down, latency p99 improved, incidents avoided) we can use as proof?
- What is the shortest integration path for an enterprise trial to validate performance within two weeks?

Next steps / owners:
- Sales engineering: assemble 1‑pager + slide kit for platform motions (Owner: Ravi).
- Product: create TCO template and get benchmark snapshots for 3 representative model families (Owner: Elena).
- GTM: run a focused outreach to 30 platform leads with the postmortem playbook and invite to a demo (Owner: Noah).

Notes and tone guidance for reps:
- Use the word "operationalize" sparingly with non‑technical buyers; lead with reliability and cost predictability.
- For engineering-focused audiences, dig into KV caching and batching as differential technical levers.
- Stay concrete: buyers trust numbers and specific rollback/canary examples more than metaphors.

This is a working draft — please push edits inline. The goal: get a concise, repeatable script that resonates with platform buyers who view LLMs less as models and more as a critical, always-on service they must protect.
